questions.prompt: A sheet resistance is quoted as \(50\ \Omega/\square\). What is the resistance of one square of that layer, of any size?
options: 50 Ω, whatever the side length
50 Ω per µm of side length
50 Ω only for a 1 µm × 1 µm square
It depends on the thickness, which the designer chooses
questions.explanation: \(R = R_\square (L/W)\); a square has \(L = W\), so \(R = R_\square\) at any size (reader Eq. 4.2). Thickness and doping are fixed by the process and folded into \(R_\square\).

questions.prompt: A layer has resistivity \(\rho = 0.012\ \Omega\,\mathrm{cm}\) and thickness \(t = 0.4\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). What is its sheet resistance in Ω/□?
questions.explanation: \[R_\square = \frac{\rho}{t} = \frac{0.012}{0.4\times10^{-4}} = 300\ \Omega/\square\] Convert µm to cm before dividing.

questions.prompt: A dog-bone resistor has a body 30 squares long, with a contact head at each end. Using the reader's rule of thumb for contact regions and \(R_\square = 80\ \Omega/\square\), what is the resistance in kΩ?
questions.explanation: Each contact region counts about 0.65 squares (reader Fig. 4.6a): \(30 + 2(0.65) = 31.3\) squares, so \(R = 31.3 \times 80 \approx 2.50\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\).

questions.prompt: Why does a right-angle corner in a constant-width resistor count as only about 0.56 squares instead of 1?
options: Corners are etched thinner
Current crowds toward the inner edge of the bend, so the corner square is not uniformly used
The outer edge of the corner has higher doping
Corners add capacitance that cancels resistance
questions.explanation: Current takes the shortest path, crowding along the inner track of the bend. The corner square therefore behaves like roughly half a square (reader Sec. 4.3.5).

questions.prompt: A serpentine resistor (constant width \(W = 2\ \mu\mathrm{m}\)) has two straight runs of \(40\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) each, joined by a short run of \(6\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) and two right-angle corners. With \(R_\square = 100\ \Omega/\square\) and ignoring contacts, find R in kΩ.
questions.explanation: Runs: \(2 \times 40/2 = 40\) squares; short run \(6/2 = 3\); corners \(2 \times 0.56 = 1.12\). Total \(44.12\) squares, so \(R \approx 4.41\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). (Run lengths are measured between corner squares.)

questions.prompt: Two resistors are drawn in the same layer: A is \(2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \times 20\ \mu\mathrm{m}\), B is \(10\ \mu\mathrm{m} \times 100\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) (width × length). How do their body resistances compare?
options: B is 5 times larger
A is 5 times larger
Equal, since both are 10 squares
B is 25 times larger
questions.explanation: Only \(L/W\) matters: \(20/2 = 100/10 = 10\) squares each. B takes 25 times the area, which is why wide resistors are used only when matching or current capacity needs them.

questions.prompt: Why is a polysilicon film resistor (on top of the oxide) preferred over a diffusion resistor when parasitics matter?
options: Poly has zero temperature coefficient
Poly resistors need no contacts
Poly has a far higher \(R_\square\) than any diffusion
Sitting on oxide, it has much less capacitance to the substrate than a reverse-biased junction
questions.explanation: A diffusion resistor's junction to the substrate is a distributed capacitor. Moving the film onto the oxide puts it farther from the substrate, lowering that capacitance (reader Sec. 4.3.2).

questions.prompt: Preview of junction capacitance: a diffusion resistor's parasitic capacitance to the substrate changes when the resistor's voltage rises (relative to the substrate). How?
options: It decreases, because the reverse bias widens the depletion region
It increases, because more charge is stored
It stays fixed, since it is set by geometry only
It changes sign
questions.explanation: The strip-substrate junction is a depletion capacitor; more reverse bias widens the depletion region and lowers \(C\).

questions.prompt: Preview of MOS resistors: in triode a MOSFET channel acts like a sheet with \(R_\square = 1/(\mu_nC_{ox}V_{ov})\). With \(\mu_nC_{ox} = 200\ \mu\mathrm{A/V^2}\) and \(V_{ov} = 0.5\ \mathrm{V}\), find \(R_\square\) in kΩ/□.
questions.explanation: \(R_\square = 1/(200\times10^{-6}\cdot0.5) = 10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}/\square\). The channel's \(R\) is then \(R_\square\cdot L/W\), and it is tuned by the gate voltage.

questions.prompt: Preview of the square law: a MOSFET's drain current is proportional to \(W/L\). In sheet-resistance language, what is \(W/L\)?
options: The number of squares in the channel
The reciprocal of the number of squares in the channel
The sheet resistance of the channel
The channel thickness divided by its length
questions.explanation: A channel \(L\) long and \(W\) wide is \(L/W\) squares; conductance scales as \(W/L\), the inverse.
